items.answer: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.
For each of the six senses, receptors are part of the sensory organs, and these receptors receive stimuli depending on the sensory organ.

The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).
Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ are bodily sensors that target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

questions.question: In the perceptual process, what must happen before perception can occur?
options: The cerebral cortex receives the external stimulus directly
Neural impulses are generated before any sense organ is stimulated
Sense organs are stimulated and convert the stimulus into neural impulses
Long-term memory alone interprets the stimulus before any sensing
questions.explanation: Perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.

questions.question: Which part of the brain is responsible for perception and also for attention, memory, language, and consciousness?
options: The axon terminals
The cerebral cortex
The dendrites
The receptors
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex is the part of the brain responsible for perception and other functions such as attention, memory, language, and consciousness.

questions.question: Why is the cerebral cortex described as a folded sheet of neurons?
options: The folding creates the gap where electrical or chemical signals pass
The folding allows the cortex to generate all sensory input directly
The folding separates sensing from perception
The folding helps fit the sheet into the skull
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex is a large, heavily folded sheet of neurons folded to fit into the skull.

data.text: Perception occurs only after sense organs are stimulated by a stimulus and convert that input into neural impulses. The cerebral cortex, containing roughly 20 billion neurons, is the part of the brain responsible for perception and other functions. It is a heavily folded sheet of neurons about 3 millimeters thick, folded to fit into the skull.
points: The perceptual process proceeds from sensing, which converts stimuli into neural impulses, to abstract perception.
The cerebral cortex contains roughly 20 billion neurons and is responsible for perception and other functions.
The cerebral cortex is a heavily folded sheet of neurons about 3 millimeters thick.

questions.question: What is the basis for perception and overall cognitive ability?
options: The isolated activity of individual neurons
The thickness of the cerebral cortex
The interconnection of neurons
The amount of muscular effort sensed by the body
questions.explanation: Perception and overall cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.

questions.question: In the directed-graph model of neuron interconnection, what does the nucleus or cell body correspond to?
options: A gap where electrical or chemical signals pass
An input edge carrying impulses toward the cell body
An output edge carrying impulses away from the cell body
A node that processes input
questions.explanation: In the directed-graph model, the nucleus or cell body is the node that processes input, while dendrites and axons are edges.

questions.question: In the directed-graph model of neuron interconnection, what do dendrites correspond to?
options: Nodes that aggregate information in the cell body
Gaps through which electrical or chemical signals pass
Output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body
Input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body
questions.explanation: Dendrites are modeled as input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body.

questions.question: How does a neuron aggregate and transmit information in the neuron-interconnection network?
options: It gathers only already-aggregated information and never receives direct neural impulses
It gathers information from other neurons through dendrites and sends the processed signal through axons
It gathers information from other neurons through axons and sends the processed signal through dendrites
It receives and sends signals only when two cell bodies are physically connected
questions.explanation: A neuron aggregates information from other neurons through its dendrites, and the processing in the cell body is transmitted through its axons.

questions.question: How does communication occur between an axon of one neuron and a dendrite of the next neuron?
options: By direct physical fusion of the axon and dendrite
By merging axon terminals from the two neurons
Across a gap called the synapse, without physical connection
By contact between the cell body of one neuron and the next
questions.explanation: An axon is paired with a dendrite, but the two are not physically connected; signals pass across the synapse.

data.text: Perception and cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons, which consist of a nucleus or cell body, dendrites, and axons. The nucleus processes input from dendrites and transmits information to other neurons through axons. Neurons communicate across a gap called a synapse, with each neuron having about 7,000 connections to form a network of 10^15 edges in the human brain.
points: Perception and cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.
A neuron consists of a nucleus or cell body, dendrites, an axon, axon branches, and axon terminals.
The nucleus processes information from dendrites and transmits it to other neurons through axons.
Neurons communicate across a gap called a synapse using electrical or chemical signals.
Each neuron has about 7,000 synaptic connections, forming a network of 10^15 edges in the human brain.

activities.title: Order the path of a neural signal

items.title: Order the path of a neural signal
steps: Dendrites carry neural impulses to the cell body
The cell body processes the input
Axons carry neural impulses from the cell body
A synapse passes electrical or chemical signals

questions.question: What is hierarchical processing?
options: The propagation of signals from the cerebral cortex back to sense organ receptors
Neural processing as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through a neural network to the cerebral cortex
The combination of real-time sensory input with knowledge stored in long-term memory
The conversion of input stimuli into neural impulses by sense organ receptors
questions.explanation: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing that occurs while receptor signals move through the neural network toward the cerebral cortex.

questions.question: How does staged aggregation work in hierarchical processing?
options: Signals are divided into lower-level details at successive levels before reaching the cerebral cortex
Signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels by neurons until the cerebral cortex is reached
Signals from receptors are combined only at the cerebral cortex
Signals from a single receptor type are copied without change until the cerebral cortex is reached
questions.explanation: Staged aggregation combines signals from many receptor types at successive neural levels, producing higher-level information rather than repeating the same lower-level information.

questions.question: What does hierarchical processing make possible in perception?
options: Detection of patterns before any neural aggregation occurs
Detection of increasingly complex patterns in the stimulus
Detection of only simple, low-level patterns in the stimulus
Detection of the same pattern complexity at every processing level
questions.explanation: Hierarchical processing allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected in the stimulus.

data.text: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex. It works by staged aggregation, in which signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels to produce higher-level information. This allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected in the stimulus.
points: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing of signals from sense organ receptors to the cerebral cortex.
Staged aggregation combines signals from various receptors at successive levels to create higher-level information.
Hierarchical processing allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected in a stimulus.

questions.question: Once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, what is combined to produce the interpretation of a stimulus?
options: Real-time sensory input and long-term memory
Real-time sensory input alone
Motor cortex efference copies
Hierarchical processing alone
questions.explanation: Interpretation is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone.

questions.question: Why can a newborn and an aged person interpret the same stimulus very differently?
options: They have different hierarchical processing stages
They have different receptor selectivity
They have different proprioception signals
They have different long-term experience
questions.explanation: The interpretation of a stimulus depends on the interpreter's long-term experience.

questions.question: Overall perceptual processing is the outcome of which combination?
options: Real-time sensory input and long-term knowledge alone
Hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge
Hierarchical processing and long-term knowledge alone
Hierarchical processing and real-time sensory input alone
questions.explanation: Overall perceptual processing results from hierarchical processing together with the combination of real-time sensory input and long-term knowledge or experience.

data.text: Interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with knowledge stored in long-term memory. This interpretation depends on a person's long-term experience. Overall, perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time input with long-term knowledge.
points: Interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with knowledge stored in long-term memory.
Interpretation of a stimulus depends on a person's long-term experience.
Perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time input with long-term knowledge.

questions.question: What is proprioception?
options: The ability to feel external touch through specialized receptors in the sense organs
The ability to interpret visual patterns by combining receptor signals in the cerebral cortex
The ability to sense relative body-part positions and the muscular effort used in moving them
The ability to detect chemical stimuli through chemoreceptors in the nasal passage
questions.explanation: Proprioception is the perception of the relative positions of body parts and the muscular effort involved in moving them.

questions.question: Why can proprioception be called a sixth sense?
options: Because the motor cortex sends efference copies to it
Because it lacks a direct sensory organ or receptor
Because it relies on chemoreceptors in the nasal passage
Because it creates a mismatch with visual input in VR
questions.explanation: It is called a sixth sense because, unlike direct perception through sensory organs, it has no direct sensory organ or receptor.

questions.question: How does the motor cortex support proprioception?
options: By sending efference copies to other brain regions to report executed motions
By balancing the various sensory inputs to prevent cybersickness in VR
By storing executed motion information in long-term memory for later use
By receiving and processing visual receptor signals in the cerebral cortex
questions.explanation: The motor cortex sends efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate what motions have been executed, and this information is processed to understand body-part positions and muscular effort.

data.text: Proprioception is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them. The motor cortex sends signals called efference copies to communicate what motions have been executed, which are then processed to understand position and effort.
points: Proprioception is the ability to sense body positions and muscular effort.
The motor cortex sends efference copies to communicate motions and help understand body position.

questions.question: Why can an immersive virtual reality system create a sensory mismatch?
options: Because the cerebral cortex instantly learns new familiar interpretations
Because the brain cannot quickly retune its long-term learned sensory processing to new inputs
Because immersive virtual reality replaces hierarchical neural processing with a simpler signal path
Because real-time sensory input alone is enough to override long-term memory
questions.explanation: An immersive VR system can interfere with the brain's long-term learned sensory processing. The brain cannot be retuned to process the new inputs in a short span of time.

questions.question: What can a sensory mismatch in virtual reality cause for a user whose brain does not adapt to it?
options: Cybersickness, including fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea
A permanent retuning of the brain's sensory processing
Uniform acceptance of the artificial experience by all users
Conscious awareness that the experience is more natural than expected
questions.explanation: A sensory mismatch may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness. Symptoms include fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

questions.question: In vection, which combination of signals creates the sensory conflict?
options: Visual input reports stillness while proprioception reports acceleration
Auditory input reports acceleration while visual input reports stillness
Visual input reports movement or acceleration while proprioception reports no motion
Proprioception reports movement while visual input reports no motion
questions.explanation: Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a person physically stationary receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration. The balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict.

questions.question: How can a sensory mismatch compromise presence in a virtual reality experience?
options: By letting the brain retune quickly and accept the experience as natural
By making the user consciously aware of the conflict and understand the experience is artificial
By strengthening the user's familiar learned sensory processing
By making the user feel the virtual environment is more real than expected
questions.explanation: A mismatch between sensory inputs and familiar processing can make the user consciously aware of the conflict. That awareness makes the user immediately understand that the experience is artificial rather than natural or real.

questions.question: What design implication follows from the need to avoid sensory conflicts in extended reality?
options: Balance the experiences presented by the various senses so the brain processes them as intended
Remove proprioceptive input so no motion can be reported
Prioritize visual stimulation alone to reduce the chance of sensory conflict
Present deliberately conflicting sensory signals to train rapid adaptation
questions.explanation: Extended reality design should carefully balance the experiences presented by the various senses. This can create an immersive experience by fooling the brain into processing information in the intended way.

data.text: The brain processes perception by combining sensory signals with long-term learned experiences, but VR systems can create sensory mismatches because the brain cannot quickly adapt to new inputs. These mismatches may be insignificant for some but can cause cybersickness or compromise the sense of presence, such as with vection where visual motion conflicts with the balance sense. XR design should balance various senses to ensure the brain processes information as intended.
points: The brain processes perception by combining sensory signals with long-term learned experiences.
VR systems can create sensory mismatches because the brain cannot quickly adapt to new inputs.
Sensory mismatches may be insignificant for some users but can cause cybersickness or compromise the sense of presence.
Vection is a sensory conflict between visual motion and the balance sense.
XR design should balance various senses to ensure the brain processes information as intended.

activities.title: Order the steps of perceptual processing

items.title: Order the steps of perceptual processing
steps: Sense organs convert the stimulus into neural impulses
Signals propagate through the neural network
Signals are aggregated at successive levels
Cortex combines input with long-term memory
Interpretation of the stimulus is produced

questions.question: How do a sense organ and the cerebral cortex work together to turn a stimulus into a perception, and why is the final interpretation not determined by sensory input alone?
questions.reference_answer: A stimulus first stimulates a sense organ, which converts that input into neural impulses, so sensing is the lowest level of the perceptual process. Hierarchical processing then combines receptor signals at successive levels until the cerebral cortex is reached, where the interpretation of the stimulus is produced. This interpretation combines real-time sensory input with long-term memory or experience, so perception is an outcome of more than the raw sensory signal alone.

questions.question: How does proprioception differ from direct perception through the five senses, and what neural signal supports it?
questions.reference_answer: Direct perception comes through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste, whereas proprioception has no direct sensory organ. It is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them. The motor cortex sends efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to report executed body motion, and this information is processed to support proprioception.

questions.question: How do presence and cybersickness explain why a VR user who is visually moving while physically stationary can feel sick or aware that the experience is artificial?
questions.reference_answer: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated, and cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness, is primarily relevant to virtual reality. Vection is an illusion of self-motion in which visual input reports movement or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory mismatch. If the user's brain cannot adapt, the mismatch can cause fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea, or it can compromise presence by making the user consciously aware that the experience is artificial.
